name: Bank Reconciliation
title: Bank Reconciliation
answer: Bank reconciliation is the process of comparing a company's internal cash records with bank statements to confirm that payments, receipts, fees, and interest are recorded correctly and that the ending balances agree. In treasury and liquidity work it covers operating accounts, payroll accounts, merchant settlement accounts, and sometimes loan or investment accounts, across multiple banks and currencies. It also includes investigating timing differences such as outstanding checks and deposits in transit, plus errors, duplicate entries, and unauthorized transactions. The scope often extends to intraday and month-end close, audit support, and cash positioning.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Bank reconciliation is the process of comparing a company's internal cash records with bank statements to confirm that payments, receipts, fees, and interest are recorded correctly and that the ending balances agree. In treasury and liquidity work it covers operating accounts, payroll accounts, merchant settlement accounts, and sometimes loan or investment accounts, across multiple banks and currencies. It also includes investigating timing differences such as outstanding checks and deposits in transit, plus errors, duplicate entries, and unauthorized transactions. The scope often extends to intraday and month-end close, audit support, and cash positioning.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Bank reconciliation runs on bank statements and transaction feeds delivered through bank portals, host-to-host connections, APIs, and standard file formats such as BAI2, MT940, CAMT, and OFX. On the company side it runs on ERP and treasury management systems, often with a general ledger, cash management module, and reconciliation subledger. Many teams still use spreadsheets for exceptions and manual matching, while larger operations use dedicated reconciliation tools or modules inside ERP suites. AI-assisted reconciliation may also run on rules engines, document parsing services, and cloud data platforms that ingest remittance advice and payment files.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with importing bank data and internal cash transactions, then normalizing dates, amounts, references, and counterparties. Rules and matching algorithms pair items by exact keys such as check number or transaction ID, then fuzzy matching and machine learning score likely matches when references are missing or inconsistent. Exceptions go to a queue where an accountant investigates, adjusts the ledger, or contacts the bank, and the reconciliation is signed off with supporting evidence. AI can also classify transactions, extract remittance details from emails or PDFs, and flag unusual patterns for review.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Governance covers who can view bank data, who can approve adjustments, and how reconciliation evidence is retained for audit and regulatory review. Provenance matters because each match should trace back to a bank statement line, a ledger entry, and the rule or model that proposed it, with version history and timestamps. Risks include false matches that hide missing cash, over-reliance on automation without sampling, unauthorized access to bank accounts, and privacy issues when payment data is used to train models. Controls typically include segregation of duties, dual approval for journal entries, audit trails, model monitoring, and periodic review of reconciliation exceptions.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Bank reconciliation is moving toward continuous, real-time matching as instant payments, open banking APIs, and ISO 20022 messaging become more common. AI models are likely to take on more exception handling, anomaly detection, and cash forecasting, while accountants focus on oversight and complex breaks. Adoption will depend on data quality, bank connectivity, and the ability to explain automated decisions to auditors and regulators. Smaller firms may see the biggest change through embedded reconciliation in accounting platforms, while large treasuries push for straight-through processing across many banks.
